implementation_notes: Sequelize is the long-standing JS ORM that gives model instances their own persistence: an instance represents one row, instance.save() inserts or updates it, instance.destroy() deletes it, instance.reload() re-reads it, and Model.create() is the shorthand for build+save - with change awareness so a save with no modifications emits no query. What replaces the classic structure is a model definition (class extends Model + init, or sequelize.define) plus promise-returning instance methods; the alternative shape is a query-builder/data-mapper stack (Knex, Prisma, Drizzle), which most TypeScript-leaning code now chooses instead.
pitfalls: Never use new User() directly - build() or create() is required, otherwise the instance is not wired to the model and saving fails.
Every persistence call is asynchronous: a missing await leaves a pending query and an unsaved row, which surfaces later as a race in tests.
save() persists the whole instance state, so values copied from a request body can overwrite columns that were never meant to change; fields/update() selects the subset.
